slides.body:
Each Boeing 737 fuselage is built in Kansas, then rides a train for about four days to Boeing near Seattle. In 2005 Boeing sold its Wichita division, which became Spirit AeroSystems, an outside supplier. Spirit went on to build 737 fuselages and major structures for the 767, 777 and 787. In December 2025 Boeing completed its purchase of Spirit's Boeing work, bringing the fuselage line back under its own roof.

The trip itself has not changed. Fuselages leave Wichita by rail and arrive in Renton, Washington, where the 737 is assembled. That one journey shows the whole map of this industry: the company whose name the plane carries, and the suppliers that build large parts of it.
slides.title: Day 1 · The map

slides.body:
The OEM is the company whose name the plane carries: Airbus, Boeing, Embraer, COMAC. It designs the aircraft, assembles it and gets the design approved. OEM stands for original equipment manufacturer. A handful of OEMs build passenger jets: Airbus and Boeing for the largest, Embraer for regional jets, and COMAC in China.

The OEM owns the design, runs final assembly and holds the regulator's type certificate, which the FAA describes as approval of the design of the aircraft and all its component parts. That makes the OEM answerable for the whole aircraft, including every part it bought from someone else.
slides.title: Layer 1 · The OEM

slides.body:
Engines, landing gear, avionics. A Tier 1 builds a complete system and sells it straight to the OEM. CFM International, owned by GE and Safran, builds LEAP engines. Collins Aerospace builds avionics, and Safran builds landing gear. Tier 1 suppliers make major components or systems: engines, control systems, landing gear, brakes, flight decks and avionics. They work directly with the OEM, often from the first design sketches of a new aircraft.

CFM International is a 50/50 joint company between GE Aerospace and Safran Aircraft Engines. Collins Aerospace, part of RTX, makes flight deck and avionics systems. Safran Landing Systems calls itself the world's largest maker of aircraft landing gear and builds the main and nose gear for the Boeing 787.
slides.title: Tier 1 suppliers deliver whole systems

slides.body:
Tier 2 makes the parts inside those systems. Tier 3 makes smaller pieces for Tier 2. Turbine blades and tires are Tier 2 work, fasteners are Tier 3. Below Tier 1 the chain gets wider. Tier 2 companies make parts or subassemblies for Tier 1: airfoils such as turbine blades, tires, structures and flight control parts. Tier 3 companies make components such as hydraulic fittings, tubing and high-strength fasteners, usually shipped to Tier 2. Each tier sells to the tier above it, not to the airline. Raw materials like aluminum, titanium and composites feed every level.

An airline almost never deals with these companies. Yet a late batch of parts deep in the chain can still hold up a finished aircraft.
slides.title: Layer 3 · Tiers 2 and 3

slides.body:
Maintenance, repair and overhaul. Airlines, engine makers and independent shops all do this work. Lufthansa Technik calls itself the world's leading independent MRO. Aviation Week has ranked AAR among the top 10 airframe MROs. Once a plane is delivered, it needs regular checks, repairs and full overhauls for the rest of its working life. Some airlines do this in-house, engine makers service their own engines, and independent MRO companies sell the work to anyone.

Lufthansa Technik describes itself as the world's leading manufacturer-independent provider of maintenance, repair and overhaul services, with more than 800 customers. AAR, based near Chicago, has been named to Aviation Week's Top 10 Airframe MROs.
slides.title: MRO keeps the plane flying after delivery

slides.body:
Call Collins a Tier 1 avionics supplier, not just an aerospace company. It tells the interviewer you know where their work fits. Each layer works differently. OEM roles touch the whole aircraft and its certification. Tier 1 roles go deep on one system and answer to OEM customers. MRO roles run on turnaround time and safety records.

Before an interview, place the company on the map and ask who its customer is. Then say it in one line: who they are, what they sell, and to whom.

exercises.explanation: Selling straight to the aircraft maker is what makes a supplier Tier 1. The OEM is the company whose name is on the plane.
